title: Beyond the AI Hype: How to Set a Modern Security Baseline (and Stay Compliant)
summary: AI has turned the security baseline from a document into a moving target. Here is how CISOs and compliance leaders in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore can keep up, and prove it.
body_markdown:
Every security team has one. A baseline: the hardened configurations, approved tools and access rules that define what “secure” looks like. It gets reviewed once a year, signed off before the audit and filed away.


Now picture an ordinary week. An analyst connects a generative AI assistant to the shared drive. A developer gives an AI agent a service account so it can close tickets on its own. A vendor switches on an AI feature inside a tool you approved two years ago. None of it raises a change request. All of it passes last year’s checklist.


The baseline says you are compliant. Are you secure? For most enterprises across Southeast Asia, nobody really knows. That gap is exactly where attackers are looking, and increasingly, where regulators are looking too.


## The static baseline was built for a world that no longer exists


Traditional baselines assume you know what is in your environment, every identity belongs to a person, and systems behave tomorrow the way they did today. AI breaks all three.


- Assets appear without asking. Employees adopt AI tools without approval, and vendors switch on AI features inside software you already use. Neither shows up in last year’s asset register.
- Identities multiply. AI agents act through API keys and service accounts, often with more access than any person would be given, and rarely with a named owner.
- Behaviour shifts. No configuration checklist can tell you whether an AI assistant will follow an instruction hidden inside a PDF.


Attackers have noticed. IBM’s 2026 breach study recorded a 56% rise in AI-driven attacks, led by deepfake impersonation and AI-enabled malware. In ASEAN, the average data breach now costs US$4.12 million, the highest IBM has recorded for the region, and nearly three in ten organisations hit by a malicious breach said the attack was AI-generated.


A baseline reviewed once a year describes an environment that no longer exists. It has to become a living system.


## Regulators have stopped asking for checklists. They want evidence.


Across the region, the rulebook is moving away from point-in-time attestation and towards continuous, demonstrable control. Indonesia’s Personal Data Protection Law requires an impact assessment whenever processing is high risk, explicitly including automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals and the use of new technology. Malaysia’s Cyber Security Act 2024 expects critical infrastructure operators to report incidents immediately, with initial details within six hours. And on 7 October 2026, MAS issued Guidelines on AI Risk Management that apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI, taking effect in October 2027.


Market What the rules now expect What your baseline must be able to show


Indonesia UU PDP: impact assessment for high-risk processing, including automated decision-making and new technology; 72-hour breach notification; fines up to 2% of annual revenue. OJK: AI governance guidance for banks. Where personal data sits, which AI systems touch it, and a current risk assessment for each.


Malaysia Cyber Security Act 2024: annual risk assessment, audit at least every two years, immediate incident notification for critical infrastructure. PDPA: 72-hour breach notification, DPO appointment. Detection fast enough to meet the clock, and evidence that controls work between audits.


Singapore Cybersecurity Act amendments: oversight of third-party-owned critical systems. MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines: supervisory expectations for all forms of AI, scaled to each institution’s risk profile, from October 2027. Visibility of every AI system in use, a risk view of each, and controls in proportion to that risk.


The common thread: a policy saying you control your AI is no longer enough. Regulators want to know what AI you run, who and what can reach your data, and proof that your controls worked yesterday, not just on audit day. Global frameworks are moving the same way, from the “Govern” function in NIST’s Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 to ISO/IEC 42001 for AI management. The smart move is to build one set of controls and map it to all of them.


## What a modern baseline looks like


A modern baseline isn’t a longer checklist. It is a set of controls that run continuously and produce evidence as they go. Five elements matter most.


*1. A live inventory that includes AI. Continuously discover models, agents, AI features inside existing software and the shadow AI your people already use. You can’t govern what you can’t see.*


*2. Identity as the control point. Give every AI agent an owner, a purpose and only the access it needs, with short-lived credentials and a record of what it did.*


*3. Controls that check themselves. Monitor for configuration drift and fix it automatically where the risk is clear, in minutes rather than at next year’s review.*


*4. Guardrails at the data boundary. Classify sensitive data and inspect what flows into and out of AI tools.*


*5. Governance with a heartbeat. Tier AI use cases by impact, review them when they change, and agree in advance who can switch a system off.*


Automation is what makes this sustainable. ASEAN organisations that used security AI and automation extensively averaged US$3.66 million per breach, against US$4.86 million for those that used none, and contained breaches 123 days faster. For a region still short of security talent, it is the only way the maths works.


## Five questions for your next compliance review


*1. Can we list every AI system in use today, including AI switched on inside vendor products?*


*2. For each one, which identities, human or machine, can reach which data?*


*3. If a regulator asked for proof that a control worked last Tuesday, how long would it take us to produce it?*


*4. Which of our controls satisfy obligations in more than one market, and where are the gaps?*


*5. Who has the authority to suspend an AI system, and have we ever tested that process?*


If any answer starts with “we’d need to check”, that is where your modern baseline begins.


## From annual sign-off to always-on assurance


The hype around AI will settle. The shift it has set off won’t. Organisations that treat compliance as a by-product of good operations, rather than a scramble before every audit, will move faster with less risk.


This is the work we do at Concentrix: running AI-driven security operations alongside governance, risk and compliance programmes, so our clients’ baselines stay current and their evidence is ready before anyone asks for it.


The question isn’t whether your baseline needs to change. It’s whether you redesign it on your own timeline, or on a regulator’s.
